---

All we know of history we learn from scenes in the mosaic of bone on the Senate floor:

The Flood turns the fields into graves, and the angels reap enough suffering to sustain them for another thousand years.

Moses tears off his beard and lights a cigarette. *I'm tired of pretending.* He shoves his box of spare commandments beneath the bed, and as he drifts toward sleep, his eyes—like caves—fill with visions of woolly rhinos.

Sailing ships crowd a small island like a forest. One light glimmers from a caravel's captain's quarters. It is Christopher Columbus. All night he has been stitching shrouds as gifts of welcome for the natives.

Little Chris presses his bleeding fingers to his lips and weeps quietly, *No one appreciates me.* God and the devil tuck him into bed. *It will get better,* they promise. Together they finish the shrouds on his behalf, while he dreams of golden nipples.

As it was, so it is now.

Spring translates the earth into hope—blades of grass taste the sea salt riding the west wind, and the blood staining soldiers' boots.

This morning, one of the old poets—an unkillable cockroach—pedaled past me, shouting, *You have the brightest light in America! Ha ha!*

On my dresser, a spider spins its web along the contours of my bra.

We lie together on the bed; I trace my hand along the muscles of your leg and feel within it eons of evolution—now outlawed by the Senate.

---

I preserved the poem's surreal juxtapositions, its dark irony, and the deliberate collision of historical/mythic imagery with intimate present-tense moments. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to tone, pacing, or specific phrases.

# The Fractured Tapestry of Time: An Analysis of Historical and Sacred Imagery

The poem constructs history not as a linear progression but as a shattered mosaic, where fragments of biblical catastrophe and modern bureaucracy collide without warning or explanation. Great floods that once cleansed the earth in Genesis exist alongside heavenly messengers and unspeakable suffering, yet these ancient sorrows bleed seamlessly into contemporary political machinery—the Senate, with its debates and procedures, becomes just another node in this vast, disordered continuum. This juxtaposition suggests that human institutions, however modern and rational they claim to be, are haunted by the same ancient violence and divine drama that shaped humanity's earliest myths. Time, in this vision, does not heal or improve; it simply repeats itself in new costumes.

## Moses: The Exhausted Prophet

Within this landscape of collapsed chronology, the poem offers a startlingly human portrait of Moses—not the towering lawgiver of scripture, but a man hollowed out by the weight of his calling. He is depicted in a moment of quiet abdication, casting aside the commandments he once carried down from the mountain with such reverence. Rather than closing his day in prayer or meditation, he lights a cigarette, a distinctly modern and mundane gesture that underscores his fall from sacred purpose into weary resignation. This Moses has grown tired of being a vessel for divine law; he wants only the small, self-destructive comfort of nicotine before sleep claims him. The image is deliberately anachronistic and deflating, stripping away the grandeur of biblical narrative to reveal a figure closer to any exhausted, disillusioned modern man.

## Columbus: The Self-Pitying Conqueror

Christopher Columbus receives a similarly unflattering, humanizing treatment. Instead of the triumphant explorer of historical mythology, he appears as an isolated and self-absorbed figure, occupied with the grim task of preparing burial shrouds for the native peoples his arrival will doom. Yet even amid this quiet complicity in genocide, his primary concern is not moral reckoning but personal validation—he yearns for recognition and praise from both God and the devil alike, as though seeking approval from every possible authority, sacred or damned. This portrayal reveals a man consumed by ego even as he stands at the threshold of historical atrocity, more concerned with his own legacy and self-image than with the human cost of his actions. His loneliness becomes almost pathetic, a hollow vanity dressed in the clothes of historical significance.

## Spring and the Cycle of Violence

The poem then shifts registers, weaving the natural imagery of springtime renewal into this same fabric of historical brutality. Traditional symbols of rebirth—blooming growth, warming light, the seasonal promise of new life—are placed in uncomfortable proximity to soldiers and bloodshed. Rather than offering solace or hope, spring becomes complicit in violence, its cyclical return mirroring the endless recurrence of war and suffering throughout human history. The natural world's rhythms and humanity's destructive tendencies are revealed as intertwined rather than opposed; renewal does not mean peace, but merely the resetting of conditions under which violence can occur again. This blending suggests a bleak determinism, where nature's beauty offers no escape from history's blood-soaked patterns.

## The Closing Intimacy: Bodies, Time, and Authority

The poem's conclusion pulls sharply inward, moving from the vast sweep of biblical and historical time to a single, intimate moment shared between two people. This tender human contact—touch, presence, closeness—becomes a vessel for contemplating deep evolutionary time, as though the connection between two bodies carries within it the entire unfolding history of the species. Yet even this private, seemingly sacred moment is not free from the reach of institutional power. The Senate reappears here, symbolizing the ways in which authority and governance intrude upon and seek to regulate even the most personal aspects of human experience—desire, touch, connection. The poem thus closes on a note of tension between intimacy and control, suggesting that no space, however private, remains untouched by the structures of power that have shaped history since its violent, fragmented beginnings.

## Conclusion

Through this collage of sacred narrative, historical figures, natural imagery, and personal intimacy, the poem constructs a vision of time as simultaneously ancient and immediate, mythic and mundane. Moses and Columbus are stripped of their heroic veneer and revealed as tired, vain, human figures; nature's renewal is exposed as complicit in violence rather than transcendent of it; and even the most private human connections remain shadowed by institutional authority. The result is a meditation on history's persistence—not as progress, but as an endless, fragmented repetition in which past and present, sacred and secular, natural and political all collapse into a single, unsettling continuum.

# The Weight of History

Moses came down from the mountain
with the tablets under his arm like grocery bags,
and God said, *You forgot the eggs,*
and Moses wept because he had carried
the whole weight of commandment
and there was still something missing.

This is how it always is with history—
someone climbs down from somewhere
holding the absolute, and it turns out
to be incomplete, or heavy in the wrong way,
or the wrong size for the shelf
where we keep our certainties.

Columbus sat on the deck of the Santa María
picking his teeth with a splinter
from the mast, watching the water
the way a man watches water
when he is tired of oceans,
when he has forgotten what he is looking for
and only remembers that he is owed something.
Land, when it came, felt like an argument
he'd already lost the taste for winning.

The devil, meanwhile, filed paperwork.
He kept meticulous records
of every soul as a kind of tax return,
deductions for suffering,
itemized griefs,
and God, across the hall,
kept asking if anyone had seen
his reading glasses,
because omniscience is a young man's game
and he was so tired,
so tired of watching
the same things happen
in different clothes.

*As it was, it is now*—
the phrase repeats like a stuck record,
like Moses forever halfway down the mountain,
like Columbus forever almost arriving,
like the devil forever collecting,
like God forever losing his glasses
in a universe he supposedly holds
in the palm of his hand.

Nothing changes except the costumes.
The violence gets a new coat of paint.
The weariness gets a new century
to wear its old face in.

And here—here is the strange thing:
last night I read that intimacy itself,
the reaching of hand toward hand,
body toward body,
the slow evolution of tenderness
into something like trust,
was outlawed by the Senate.

Just like that. A vote.
A show of hands
to prohibit the show of hands.

And I thought of Moses on the mountain,
of Columbus on the water,
of God losing his glasses,
of the devil with his ledgers—
how power has always wanted
to legislate the space between two people,
to draw a line through touch,
to make evolution itself
a criminal act,
because a species that learns to hold on
to one another
is a species that stops
needing to be ruled.

*As it was, it is now.*

The tablets get carried down again.
The ships keep almost-arriving.
The paperwork keeps piling up
in the devil's office,
and God keeps searching
for what he's lost,
and somewhere a law is passed
against the ancient, animal miracle
of one hand finding another
in the dark—

and we call this history,
we call this progress,
we call this, God help us,
civilization.

# The Senate: An Institution for All

The Senate stands as one of the most enduring institutions in American governance, embodying principles that have shaped the nation's legislative process for over two centuries. As the upper chamber of Congress, the Senate was designed to serve as a deliberative body where careful consideration and debate could temper the passions of popular opinion.

The founders envisioned the Senate as a place where all states, regardless of size or population, would receive equal representation. This design reflects a fundamental compromise reached during the Constitutional Convention—ensuring that smaller states would have a voice equal to that of their larger counterparts. Each state sends two senators to Washington, D.C., a structure that remains unchanged since the nation's founding.

The Senate's responsibilities extend across numerous critical functions. It confirms presidential appointments, ratifies treaties, and serves as the venue for impeachment trials. These powers underscore the chamber's role as a check on executive authority and a guardian of institutional balance within the federal government.

Throughout history, the Senate has been the site of some of the nation's most consequential debates. From discussions on civil rights to matters of war and peace, senators have used this platform to advocate for their constituents while grappling with issues that affect all Americans. The chamber's traditions—including extended debate and the filibuster—reflect a commitment to ensuring that minority viewpoints receive a hearing, even when majority opinion might otherwise prevail.

Critics and supporters alike recognize that the Senate, for all its imperfections, remains central to American democracy. Its emphasis on deliberation, compromise, and equal state representation continues to shape how the nation addresses its most pressing challenges, making it an institution truly meant to serve the interests of all citizens across the country.

**The Ships Have Names Like Committees**

Columbus kneels in the Senate cloakroom,
wringing seawater from the flag,
counting islands he has not yet stolen
into the record, into the eternal record,
where the clerk—who is also Moses,
who is also nobody, who is also
your uncle who believes in nothing
but the stock ticker—
transcribes the murmuring of locusts
as *yeas* and *nays*.

The Red Sea does not part anymore.
It simply recesses,
gavel-struck, into two coasts
that argue about who owns the water
that owns nobody.

I saw Moses on C-SPAN at 3 a.m.,
his staff replaced by a pointer,
tapping a chart of GDP
shaped like a burning bush
that refuses, politely, to be consumed
or debated further—
tabled, in fact, until next session,
until the manna turns to omnibus,
until the forty years become
a filibuster with better lighting.

Columbus keeps a globe in his coat pocket,
spins it like a roulette wheel,
lands his finger always
on somebody else's country,
declares it discovered,
declares it *bipartisan*,
plants a flag made of subpoenas
in soil that was never asking
to be found.

And God, who I think is a senior senator
from a state that no longer exists
except in the Constitution's fine print,
clears His throat like thunder
clears a hallway,
says: *Let there be order,*
and there is instead
a quorum call
that stretches into forty years
of wandering committee rooms
looking for a promised land
that turns out to be
a parking garage
under the Capitol,
where Moses waits with tablets
nobody will yield the floor to read,

where Columbus still believes
he's almost to India,
where the locusts vote present,
where the burning bush
just wants a fair hearing,
where somewhere in Leviticus
it says *do not covet your neighbor's subcommittee,*

and nobody
is listening,
and everybody
is discovered,
and the sea,
tired of dividing,
just sits there
being water,
being older
than all of this,
being the only witness
that isn't sworn in.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental prose-poem that mixes creation myths, colonial history, and intimate present-tense scenes, using dreamlike, fragmented imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the River Remembers Before It Is Named

*In the beginning there was a mouth and the mouth was water and the water said let there be division—*

I.

Before the ships, the water had no edges. Ask the old women. Ask the stone that used to be a woman before she sat down and forgot to get up. *In the beginning* is a phrase that assumes a middle and an end, assumes a line, assumes someone standing outside of time holding a pen.

The pen arrives in 1497. The pen arrives wearing wool in equatorial heat. The pen writes *discovered* over a word that already existed in another mouth.

*Let there be light,* says the ledger. *Let there be inventory.*

II.

You are washing dishes in a kitchen that does not yet exist in the myth. Your hands are wet the way the first hands were wet, coming up out of clay, out of rib, out of whatever story your mother told you before she told you the other one, the true one, the one about her mother's mother crossing water that was not a metaphor.

The window above the sink holds a square of sky. The sky does not remember 1619. The sky is very good at forgetting, or perhaps it is very good at holding everything at once, the way a mouth can hold both a name and its erasure.

III.

*And the serpent said: you will not surely die.*

But some did. Some died in the hold, in the space between decks that was thirty inches high, was a kind of second creation, dark and wet and no light moving on the face of those waters, no spirit hovering, only weather, only weight, only the manifest listing bodies as barrels, as board feet, as *goods.*

This is also a creation story. This is how new gods were made: by grinding old ones down to cargo, by baptizing the drowned with new names in the ship's log.

*In the beginning was the Word,* and the Word was *property,* and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld its glory, full of grace and truth and chains.

IV.

Now: your daughter asks why the sky is blue and you say *light bends* and she asks *why does it bend* and you don't have the myth for this, you only have physics, which is also a kind of creation story, wavelengths scattering like a diaspora, like a people finding the color that survives the furthest distance.

You want to tell her: *once there was no blue. Once there was only the water's memory of itself, dark and original, and someone came with a flag and said this water is now called ocean, this ocean is now called route, this route is now called trade.*

You don't tell her this. You tell her *because science.* You tuck her in. The night outside continues its old argument with the light.

V.

*Genesis 1:2 — the earth was without form, and void.*

Which is also how the census described the land before the treaty. Which is also how the surveyor described the valley before the railroad. Which is also how the coroner described the body before the verdict.

*Void* is a word that requires forgetting what was already full.

VI.

I am trying to write a creation myth that is also a history that is also this Tuesday, the coffee going cold, the radiator's small argument with silence, my grandmother's hands which I remember though she died before I could ask her the questions that matter—

*what did the water sound like before they named it Middle Passage*

*what does clay remember about being lifted into shape*

*who blew breath into the first body and did that body ask to be made*

VII.

Here is what I know: creation is never singular. It happens in the ship's hold and in the kitchen and in the space between question and answer where a child waits for a myth to make sense of blue.

Here is what I know: colonization is a false creation story, a man saying *let there be* over a world that already *was.*

Here is what I know: I am dust and I am also the hand that shapes dust and I am also the argument about whose hand gets to shape.

VIII.

*In the beginning was water, and the water had a name, and the name was taken, and the water kept moving anyway, the way blood keeps moving, the way memory keeps moving under the floor of language, dark and unbaptized and entirely its own.*

Wash the dishes. Watch the window. Somewhere, still, someone is naming the world for the first time, and somewhere, still, someone is being erased by that naming, and these are happening in the same instant, the same breath, the mouth of the river opening and closing, opening and closing, saying *and saying and saying.*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Republic of Broken Mirrors

In the beginning was the Word,
and the Word was branded,
trademarked, sold at auction
to the highest-bidding tongue.

Moses came down from the mountain
carrying tablets of stone,
but the golden calf had learned to speak
in a Southern drawl, promising
to make the wilderness great again.
The Israelites wept not from guilt
but from the commercial breaks.

*

George Washington crosses the Delaware
forever, an eternal GIF,
his wooden teeth grinding
prophecies about cherry trees
that never existed, axes
that cut down nothing
but the truth, which was already
hollow, already a stage prop
in a play with no author,
only investors.

*

Judas didn't hang himself—
he ran for office,
was elected twice,
his thirty pieces of silver
multiplied into a Super PAC,
his kiss on Christ's cheek
replayed on every channel
as a "moment of unity,"
a "bipartisan embrace,"
while the crowd cheered
for the crucifixion
because it was must-see TV,
because Barabbas
had better ratings,
better hair,
a healthier relationship
with the cameras.

*

Lincoln's log cabin
is a Airbnb now,
five stars, "rustic charm,"
the ghost of abolition
serving complimentary champagne
to senators who still
count in fractions,
still measure worth
in the currency of skin,
still speak of freedom
like a word they found
in their grandfather's coat pocket,
crumpled, unspendable,
but nice to hold.

*

The serpent in the garden
didn't tempt Eve with fruit—
it tempted her with a headline,
a scroll, an endless feed
of apples that were always
almost the truth,
always red enough
to bite, and God
didn't banish them from Eden,
He just changed the terms of service,
buried the eviction notice
in fine print
no one had time to read
because the world was ending
in fourteen-minute increments,
sponsored by a war
that never officially began
and therefore
could never officially end.

*

And in the desert, forty days,
forty nights, the devil
took the candidate
to a very high mountain,
showed him all the kingdoms
of cable news,
said: *all this I will give you,
if you'll just kneel
before the teleprompter,
if you'll just let me
write your name in gold
across the sky*—

and the candidate did not say
*get thee behind me.*
He said: *can we get a deal
on the naming rights?*

*

This is the gospel
according to nobody,
the history according
to the shredded document,
the myth we keep re-enacting
in courtrooms, in parking lots
outside gun shows, in the space
between the flag and the folding
of the flag, in the silence
after the anthem
when someone always asks,
too loud, too late:

*wait—
whose blood is this,
and why does it taste
like advertising?*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long-form poem that juxtaposes Old Testament imagery, Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas, and a tender modern love scene, ending with a reference to legislation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Covenant Waters**

**I. In the Beginning There Was Water**

Before the first light split the dark like a seam,
the Spirit moved upon the face of the waters,
brooding the way a woman broods
over a bowl of dough left to rise in silence.
God said *let there be*, and there was,
and it was good, and it was good,
until it wasn't — until the fountains
of the great deep broke open
and forty days became a verdict,
and the ark rode the flood
like a promise nobody trusted yet,
Noah counting ravens, counting doves,
counting the days until an olive leaf
proved the world had somewhere left to stand.

**II. Landfall, 1492**

Three ships and a captain's log:
*Tierra! Tierra!* a sailor screamed at moonrise,
mistaking a bonfire on the shore
for the pillar of fire that led another people
out of one bondage into another.
Columbus fell to his knees in the sand
the way Noah fell to his knees on Ararat,
and named what already had a name —
called it *San Salvador*, Holy Savior,
as if salvation were a flag
you could plant in another man's chest.
He wrote of gold and gentleness
in the same ink, the same breath,
of natives "fit to be ordered about,"
and did not hear, in his own testament,
the echo of the oldest line in scripture:
*you shall be as gods, knowing.*
He named the doves. He kept the gold.
The rainbow, when it came, was not a promise.
It was a survey line.

**III. A Small Room, Tonight**

Meanwhile, in no century in particular,
a man traces the coastline of a woman's spine
the way a cartographer traces a border
he has no intention of crossing without her leave.
*I am my beloved's,* she does not say aloud,
but the lamp says it for her, low and gold.
She is not a continent. She is not new world
or old. She is only herself,
turning toward him in the dark
the way the dove turned back to the ark
with green still in her mouth —
proof that somewhere the water had gone down,
that somewhere dry land remembered how to hold a root.
He says her name like a small prayer
that doesn't ask for anything,
only says: *you again, you still, you here.*
This is the whole of scripture he can manage tonight —
not dominion, not discovery,
just his hand finding the exact latitude
of her hand, and staying there,
unclaimed, unflagged, unmapped.

**IV. What We Named and What We Took**

But history does not let the small room stay small.
Outside the window, ships still arrive
somewhere, always, and someone kneels
in sand that isn't his,
writing of gentleness and gold
in the same paragraph, the same breath.
The old god drowned a world to start again
and called it mercy.
The new world's god drowned a world to start again
and called it progress.
Both floods recede. Both leave a rainbow
someone will later survey, someone will later patent,
someone will later write into a book of law
so fine print swallows the sky it came from.

**V. Public Law**

And it came to pass, in the second session
of a congress no prophet foresaw,
that the following was enacted:

*Be it resolved that land shall mean
whatever the surveyor's map says it means.
Be it resolved that arrival shall be called discovery
if the arriving hand holds a sword,
and called illegal if it holds only a child.
Be it resolved that love, to be recognized,
must be filed in triplicate,
witnessed, stamped, entered into the record
by five o'clock, business days only.*

Section 12. This Act shall take effect immediately
and shall bind all waters, all coastlines,
all beds where two people once lay
believing themselves, for one green-mouthed moment,
ungoverned.

# Cartography of Wounds

The gods came first, always the gods,
riding in on ships with names like prayers—
*Santa María*, *Trinidad*, *Victoria*—
as if violence needed christening
to become holy.

I think of Coatlicue, skirt of serpents,
her necklace of hands and hearts,
how they called her monster
before they called her ours to unmake.
How easily the sacred becomes
specimen becomes
souvenir.

*

You touch me like a man reading a map
he did not draw,
tracing borders that existed
before your hands knew hunger,
and I let you,
because some nights I am tired
of being the whole continent,
tired of my body as allegory,
as resource,
as thing to be discovered
and named after men
who were lost the entire time.

*

Prometheus gave fire and got the liver torn out
daily, an eternal harvest—
but what do we call it
when the theft is the land itself,
when the vulture wears a crucifix,
when they leave you the myth
of your own gratitude?

*

My grandmother's grandmother
prayed to saints she did not choose,
her tongue rearranged
like furniture in a house
that was never hers to arrange,
Nahuatl folding into Spanish
folding into silence
folding into me,
three generations later,
still finding the seams.

*

In bed you ask what I'm thinking
and I say *nothing*
because how do I tell you
that your hand on my hip
feels like a flag planted,
feels like Malinche's confession,
feels like the moment before
the word *pacification*
enters the history books
smooth and bloodless
as a communion wafer?

*

Icarus fell because he flew too close—
but some of us
were pushed from the temples,
were told the fall was
our own design,
our own hubris,
when it was only ever
gravity and greed
wearing each other's clothes.

*

I want to love you
without translating myself first.
I want my mouth to be
just a mouth,
not a border crossing,
not a treaty being renegotiated
with every kiss.

*

The old gods are patient.
They wait in the blood
like something dormant,
like Quetzalcoatl coiled
in the marrow,
waiting to remember
he was never a snake at all—
just a story
they needed him to be
so the sword could make sense
of itself.

*

Tonight, touch me
like I am not a metaphor.
Touch me like the myths are just stories
and not maps,
like history is a country
we get to leave,
like intimacy doesn't have to mean
someone plants a flag
and someone else
learns to call it home.
